title: Negative Pell x² − 2y² = −1: The Linear Recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ of the Solution Chain
description: The parent (oq-06) defines the chain of solutions of x² − 2y² = −1 by the first-order vector recurrence (xₙ₊₁, yₙ₊₁) = (3xₙ + 4yₙ, 2xₙ + 3yₙ) — iteration of the transfer matrix M = [[3,4],[2,3]]. This entry records the scalar shadow: each coordinate, on its own, satisfies the second-order linear recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ. The coefficients (6, 1) are exactly (tr M, det M); the characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 = 0 has roots 3 ± 2√2 (the units ζ², ζ⁻² of the sibling oq-02), reflecting the Cayley–Hamilton relation M² = 6M − I. The recurrences are proved directly from the parent's definition by a one-step ring identity, and the recurrence together with the two initial values is shown to characterize each coordinate sequence uniquely.

meta.author: Lean Genius (linear-recurrence / Cayley–Hamilton shadow); classical theory
originalContributions: negPellSeq_fst_rec: the first coordinates satisfy xₙ₊₂ = 6xₙ₊₁ − xₙ — the scalar order-2 recurrence whose characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 is that of the transfer matrix [[3,4],[2,3]] (trace 6, determinant 1); proved by expanding two steps of the parent's vector recurrence and one ring identity
negPellSeq_snd_rec: the second coordinates satisfy the same recurrence yₙ₊₂ = 6yₙ₊₁ − yₙ — both coordinates obey the relation dictated by Cayley–Hamilton M² = 6M − I

negPellSeq_fst_unique: the recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ together with u₀ = 1, u₁ = 7 determines the first-coordinate sequence — a two-step induction characterizing the chain by its recurrence and initial data
negPellSeq_snd_unique: the companion characterization for the y-values (initial data u₀ = 1, u₁ = 5)
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-checked: 0 axioms, 0 sorries, no native_decide (the uniqueness base cases use kernel `decide` on concrete chain values, not `native_decide`). Imports the parent file Proofs/PellEquationOQ06.lean to reuse the chain negPellSeq and its one-step recurrence negPellSeq_succ.

crossReferences.description: The parent defines the chain by the first-order vector recurrence (multiplication by the matrix [[3,4],[2,3]]). This entry derives the equivalent second-order scalar recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ obeyed by each coordinate separately, and shows it characterizes the sequences uniquely from their initial values.

The sibling realizes the chain as the odd powers of the fundamental unit ζ = 1 + √2 of ℤ[√2]. The eigenvalues 3 ± 2√2 of the transfer matrix here are exactly ζ² and ζ⁻²; the characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 is the minimal polynomial of ζ² over ℚ. The two entries give the matrix/recurrence and the ring/unit views of the same structure.

overview.historicalContext: Solutions of Pell-type equations have been generated by linear recurrences since Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II: once a fundamental solution and the recurrence are known, all chain members follow by simple integer arithmetic, with no square roots. For x² − 2y² = −1 the transfer is the matrix M = [[3,4],[2,3]] of the fundamental unit 3 + 2√2 of ℤ[√2]; its characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 (trace 6, determinant 1) encodes the order-2 recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ that every coordinate satisfies. This is the discrete analogue of the Cayley–Hamilton theorem M² − (tr M)M + (det M)I = 0, here giving a purely arithmetic generation rule whose convergents 1, 7, 41, 239, … and 1, 5, 29, 169, … are the numerators and denominators of the continued-fraction approximants to √2.
overview.problemStatement: The parent generates the chain by the coupled first-order recurrence (xₙ₊₁, yₙ₊₁) = (3xₙ + 4yₙ, 2xₙ + 3yₙ). Can each coordinate be generated on its own, decoupled from the other? Concretely: does each of (xₙ) and (yₙ) satisfy a single second-order linear recurrence, and is that recurrence (with the initial data) enough to pin the sequence down?
overview.proofStrategy: Expand two steps of the parent's vector recurrence: xₙ₊₂ = 3xₙ₊₁ + 4yₙ₊₁ and substitute xₙ₊₁ = 3xₙ + 4yₙ, yₙ₊₁ = 2xₙ + 3yₙ; the yₙ terms cancel against 6xₙ₊₁ − xₙ, leaving the identity xₙ₊₂ = 6xₙ₊₁ − xₙ (and symmetrically for yₙ), discharged by `ring` after `simp only [negPellSeq_succ]`. For uniqueness, a two-step induction tracks the pair (uₙ = xₙ, uₙ₊₁ = xₙ₊₁): the base case matches the initial values, and the step rewrites uₙ₊₂ by the recurrence, substitutes both inductive hypotheses, and closes with negPellSeq_fst_rec.
keyInsights: The coupled first-order vector recurrence and the single second-order scalar recurrence are equivalent descriptions of the same orbit; eliminating one variable raises the order by one, exactly as Cayley–Hamilton predicts for a 2×2 transfer matrix.

The recurrence coefficients are not arbitrary: 6 = tr M and 1 = det M for M = [[3,4],[2,3]]. The characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 has roots 3 ± 2√2, the conjugate fundamental units of ℤ[√2] (the squares ζ², ζ⁻² of the unit ζ = 1 + √2 in the sibling entry).

Both coordinates satisfy the SAME recurrence; they differ only in initial data (1, 7 for x; 1, 5 for y). This is forced because both are linear functionals of the matrix-power orbit Mⁿ, which Cayley–Hamilton annihilates by t² − 6t + 1.

A linear recurrence plus initial data is a complete description: negPellSeq_fst_unique/snd_unique show any integer sequence with the right two seeds and the recurrence equals the chain coordinate, so the convergents 1, 7, 41, 239, … (resp. 1, 5, 29, 169, …) are determined with no reference to the original Diophantine equation.

sections.title: Module Header and Research Context
sections.summary: Explains that the parent uses a first-order vector recurrence (transfer matrix [[3,4],[2,3]]) and that this entry derives the second-order scalar recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ obeyed by each coordinate, with coefficients (tr M, det M) = (6, 1) forced by Cayley–Hamilton.
sections.mathContext: Transfer matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, $\operatorname{tr}M=6$, $\det M=1$, characteristic polynomial $t^2-6t+1$ with roots $3\pm2\sqrt2$.

sections.title: The second-order recurrence for each coordinate
sections.summary: negPellSeq_fst_rec proves xₙ₊₂ = 6xₙ₊₁ − xₙ and negPellSeq_snd_rec proves the identical recurrence for yₙ, each by expanding two steps of the parent's vector recurrence and a single ring identity.

sections.title: The recurrence and initial data characterize the chain
sections.summary: negPellSeq_fst_unique and negPellSeq_snd_unique show that the recurrence uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ together with the two initial values (1, 7 for x; 1, 5 for y) determines the coordinate sequence uniquely, by a two-step induction.
sections.mathContext: A second-order linear recurrence with two seeds has a unique solution; tracking the pair $(u_n,u_{n+1})$ in the induction closes the step via negPellSeq_fst_rec.

sections.title: Sanity checks against the explicit chain
sections.mathContext: Convergents of $\sqrt2$: $x_n = 1,7,41,239,\dots$ and $y_n = 1,5,29,169,\dots$, each generated by $u_{n+2}=6u_{n+1}-u_n$.

conclusion.summary: This fully verified 129-line file (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) extracts the scalar linear recurrence hidden in the parent's vector construction: each coordinate of the negative-Pell chain satisfies uₙ₊₂ = 6uₙ₊₁ − uₙ, the recurrence whose characteristic polynomial t² − 6t + 1 is that of the transfer matrix [[3,4],[2,3]] (trace 6, determinant 1). The recurrence is proved by a one-step ring identity from the parent's definition, and shown — via a two-step induction — to characterize each coordinate sequence uniquely from its initial values.
conclusion.implications: Reducing the coupled first-order system to a single second-order recurrence is the Cayley–Hamilton theorem in action and makes the chain computable by pure integer arithmetic, no square roots. It also ties together the two structural views of this lineage: the matrix/recurrence picture here and the ring/unit picture of the sibling oq-02, whose units ζ², ζ⁻² are precisely the roots 3 ± 2√2 of the characteristic polynomial.
openQuestions: Promote the scalar recurrence to its matrix origin: prove M² = 6M − I for M = [[3,4],[2,3]] using Mathlib's Matrix.charpoly / Cayley–Hamilton, and derive negPellSeq_fst_rec/snd_rec uniformly as the action of that relation on the state vector.
Give the closed form uₙ = A(3+2√2)ⁿ + B(3−2√2)ⁿ via the characteristic roots, recovering the sibling oq-02's powers-of-the-unit description as the solution of the recurrence.
Generalize: for x² − Dy² = −1 (solvable D) the coordinates satisfy uₙ₊₂ = 2x₁·uₙ₊₁ − uₙ where (x₁, y₁) is the fundamental norm +1 unit; formalize the trace coefficient uniformly in D.
